tur62-0: What is teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism), how much force acts on the teeth, and how are the teeth, joint, neck and brain affected? Its links with migraine and fibromyalgia, psychological factors, the place of the splint, multidisciplinary treatment, botulinum toxin, jaw dislocation, history and eight exercises at home.
tur62-1: Tooth marks on the tongue and other signs
tur62-3: Clenching and grinding can lead to tooth wear, sensitivity to hot and cold, broken fillings and teeth, cracks in the teeth and problems with dentures. There are clues inside the mouth too: in a 2026 study of 98 patients in Türkiye, among those with bruxism confirmed by a sleep study, 65.3% had tooth marks on the edges of the tongue and 75.5% had a white line on the inside of the cheek along the level of the teeth. The dentist examines tooth wear and the bite (occlusion); however, the bite is no longer seen as the main cause of bruxism. The signs inside the mouth are described in detail in the tooth marks on the tongue and other signs section below.
tur62-4: One possible explanation for this link lies in the nervous system: in a group of nerve cells called the trigeminocervical complex, nerves carrying pain signals from the head and nerves from the upper neck converge on the same nerve cells. This convergence is thought to contribute to pain spreading between the head and neck and being felt somewhere else (referred pain). It has been suggested that this mechanism may also contribute to jaw and neck pain occurring together.
tur62-5: During the years I worked with Cihan Hoca, we saw teeth clenching in many of the patients who came to us with neck pain that had not resolved despite previous treatments. Today, too, many people turn to one treatment after another for complaints such as waking up tired, morning headaches, and neck and shoulder pain; in clinic I see that teeth clenching can sometimes turn out to be behind these complaints. In advanced cases that do not settle, I also come across pain that spreads from the neck to the arm and resembles nerve root compression but is not true root compression. You can read what nerve root compression is in the cervical disc herniation guide. I share these as my own clinical observations, not as research findings; not everyone may respond in the same way.
tur62-7: Tooth marks on the tongue, a line on the cheek and other signs
tur62-8: Many people who clench their teeth do not know it; but the mouth and face often give clues. In the 2018 international consensus, the signs looked for on examination for "probable" bruxism include tooth marks on the tongue or lip, a white line on the inside of the cheek, enlargement of the chewing muscles, mechanical tooth wear, cracked teeth, and fillings or dentures that fail again and again.
tur62-9: Tooth marks on the tongue: indentations along the edges of a tongue pushed against the teeth during clenching (schematic, top view)
tur62-10: Arrows: During clenching, the tongue is pushed against the teeth.
tur62-11: Tongue edge: The inner surfaces of the teeth can leave a row of indentations along both sides of the tongue (scalloped tongue). The drawing is schematic.
tur62-12: Tooth marks on the tongue (scalloped tongue)
tur62-13: A row of indentations along both side edges of the tongue, at the level of the teeth, is called a scalloped tongue. Because the tongue is pushed against the teeth again and again during clenching, the inner surfaces of the teeth can leave marks on the edge of the tongue. In the 2026 study in Türkiye, 65.3% of those with bruxism confirmed by a sleep study had tooth marks on the edges of the tongue, compared with 34.7% of those who only reported clenching themselves.
tur62-14: However, these marks are not specific to clenching. The consensus report notes that marks on the tongue and cheek can also result from ordinary mouth movements such as swallowing. A wide tongue, a habit of pushing the tongue against the teeth and structural differences in the teeth can also cause a scalloped tongue. In a 2025 study of 160 patients who had a full sleep study, most of them referred with suspected sleep apnoea, a scalloped tongue was seen in about half of the patients; those with a scalloped tongue were about 3 times more likely to have severe sleep apnoea. So if you have marks on your tongue and you snore, or someone has told you that your breathing stops during sleep, be sure to tell your physician.
tur62-16: A white line on the cheek
tur62-18: A white line on the inside of the cheek, running along the level of the back teeth. It can form from the pressure of the cheeks against the teeth during clenching and grinding. In the 2026 study it was seen in 75.5% of those with confirmed bruxism.
tur62-21: A chewing muscle that works constantly can thicken over time. If one side is more dominant during grinding, the enlargement may be on one side only.
tur62-22: Signs of wear on the teeth
tur62-24: Flattened wear facets on the teeth and excessive wear of the front teeth; sometimes notches in the part of the tooth near the gum (abfraction). These notches can also have other causes.
tur62-27: Cracks in the teeth, and fillings and dentures that break or come out again and again.
tur62-30: A headache felt on waking; tiredness, pain or stiffness in the jaw.
tur62-33: Stick out your tongue and look at both side edges: are there wavy indentations at the level of the teeth?
tur62-35: Look inside your cheek: is there a white line along the level of your back teeth?
tur62-37: Clench your teeth lightly and feel the chewing muscle in your cheeks with both hands: is the muscle hard or tender, and do the two sides feel different?
tur62-38: Do you have jaw tiredness or a headache when you wake up? Does your bed partner hear grinding?
tur62-39: This check does not make a diagnosis. If you have one or more of these signs, you can see your dentist, and if you also have jaw and neck pain, a physiotherapist or physician.
tur62-40: Jaw dislocation: if the mouth stays open
tur62-41: The jaw joint can come out of place when the mouth is opened very wide (such as yawning, laughing, singing or vomiting), during dental treatment or after a blow to the face; it most often dislocates forwards. The mouth stays open and will not close; there may be pain in front of the ear, difficulty speaking and drooling. If the dislocation is on one side, the jaw shifts to one side.
tur62-44: Go to the emergency department straight away. Do not try to force the jaw back into place yourself or let someone close to you do so; before it is put back, it may need to be checked for a fracture.
tur62-47: In the best-known method, the physician places their thumbs on the lower back teeth and pushes the jaw first downwards and then backwards to put the joint back in place. When needed, medication or sedation is used to reduce pain, anxiety and muscle spasm.
tur62-49: Not opening the mouth more than 2 cm, supporting the jaw with the hand when yawning and eating soft foods for between a few days and two weeks are recommended; a check-up with ear, nose and throat or oral and maxillofacial surgery within 2–3 days is recommended.
tur62-52: Having had a dislocation before, excessive mobility of the jaw joint and some conditions affecting connective tissue can increase the risk of dislocation and recurrence. Repeated dislocations can damage the joint ligaments and capsule; in that case a specialist assessment is needed.
tur62-53: In stressful or tense moments many people clench their teeth without noticing. Patient leaflets also state that emotional stress can show itself as teeth clenching and that tension can increase jaw pain. According to a review of 45 papers, daytime clenching in particular (awake bruxism) appears to be associated with psychosocial factors and some psychological symptoms; associations with anxiety, stress sensitivity, depression and some personality traits have been reported. For sleep bruxism, however, no evidence supporting a link with psychosocial problems was found. The authors note that most of the data reporting a link are based on clinical examination or people's own reports, while sleep laboratory studies conflict with these findings.
tur62-55: In a systematic review, people with stress were about twice as likely to have bruxism (low certainty of evidence). The studies in the review looked at different types of stress, such as work stress and stressful life events.
tur62-57: A tendency to anxiety and sensitivity to stress are described as the main psychological factors linked with bruxism, both in children and adolescents and in adults.
tur62-59: A link with depression has been reported; anxiety and depression are also common in people with jaw joint pain.
tur62-62: It has been suggested that people prone to anxiety and negative emotions (neuroticism), with a strong sense of responsibility and anxious expectations, may release emotional tension by clenching or grinding their teeth; this is not yet a proven finding but a hypothesis.
tur62-63: Mood, clenching and pain affect one another
tur62-64: In a meta-analysis combining 20 studies, people with bruxism were about 2.2 times more likely to have a jaw joint disorder, and 2.5 times more likely with awake bruxism. Jaw joint pain is also associated with anxiety and depression. These links may point to a vicious circle: stress can increase clenching, clenching can increase pain, and pain can in turn increase stress. However, these studies do not show the direction of the relationship for certain. This is why treatment addresses not only the teeth and muscles but also mood.
tur62-67: Observe in which situations during the day you clench: work, traffic, screen time, arguments or moments of worry.
tur62-69: In a quiet place, put your hands on your belly and breathe slowly and deeply through your nose; practise for about 5 minutes. Once you have learned it, you can use it whenever you feel tense.
tur62-70: Regular movement and a sleep routine
tur62-71: Regular exercise can help you relax. Improving your sleep by going to bed at the same time every night is also among the steps recommended to reduce teeth grinding.
tur62-73: If anxiety, depression or sleep problems are marked, seek psychiatric or psychological support; cognitive behavioural therapy is one of these approaches. According to the authors of a systematic review, approaches that include relaxation training or biofeedback may reduce stress-related muscle activity, especially in awake bruxism; however, the certainty of the evidence is very low.
tur62-75: Awake bruxism often happens without your noticing. In a study in which 46 dental students reported the state of their jaw at that moment through a smartphone app 15 times a day at random times for one week, the jaw muscles were relaxed in 71.7% of responses. The most common behaviours were the teeth touching (14.5%) and clenching the jaw without the teeth touching (10%). When clenching and grinding of the teeth were added, an awake bruxism behaviour was present in about 28% of moments during the day in these healthy young adults. To observe yourself, you can ask a few times a day: "Are my teeth touching right now?"
tur62-76: Eight exercises for the jaw and neck
tur62-77: Do the movements slowly, within a pain-free range. If pain increases, stop and consult a physiotherapist or physician. Sliding the jaw side to side and pushing it forwards also work the jaw in directions other than opening and closing. If you have recently had a jaw dislocation, do not open your mouth more than 2 cm in the first 1–3 weeks; start the exercises on the advice of your physician or physiotherapist.
tur62-78: Sliding the jaw side to side
tur62-79: Part your lips slightly. Slowly slide your lower jaw to the left, hold for 10 seconds and return to the middle; do the same to the right. Make sure the movement comes from your jaw, not your lips, and stay within a pain-free range.
tur62-82: Part your lips slightly. Push your jaw forwards so that your lower jaw comes in front of your upper jaw. Hold for 5–10 seconds and return to the resting position. If there is pain or catching, do not force it.

In a 2026 study of 98 patients in Türkiye, 65.3% of those with bruxism confirmed by a sleep study had tooth marks on the edges of the tongue, compared with 34.7% of those who only reported clenching themselves. A white line on the inside of the cheek along the level of the teeth was seen in 75.5% and 42.9% respectively. These signs do not make a diagnosis on their own: marks on the tongue and cheek can also result from ordinary mouth movements such as swallowing. Marks on the tongue may also be related to a wide tongue or structural differences in the teeth, and in one study they were associated with severe sleep apnoea. They are assessed together with a dental examination; if you also snore, tell your physician.
